summary: Point Iroquois Light, first built in 1855 and rebuilt in brick in 1870, guided ships into the St. Marys River until the Coast Guard closed it in 1962. A Forest Service site with a seasonal tower.

lens.where: Removed from the lantern in the early 1960s and shipped to the Smithsonian Institution (Terry Pepper; LighthouseFriends); the display there was not checked

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record gives 1855 (Rowlett's directory). Terry Pepper gives the first exhibition as 8 June 1856 and the Forest Service as 20 September 1857. The 1855 date is the construction year on the Forest Service and Terry Pepper pages; the first lighting is not settled by the sources read.

The record gives the brick tower as built 1856. Terry Pepper, the Forest Service, the marker and LighthouseFriends all date the standing brick tower to 1870; the 1855-56 tower was rubble stone with a wooden lantern deck.

Terry Pepper says the Coast Guard transferred the station to the U.S. Park Service in 1965. LighthouseFriends, the marker and the Forest Service all name the Forest Service (Hiawatha National Forest).

corrections.why: The Coast Guard decommissioned the light in 1962 (marker) and Terry Pepper says it was discontinued after a lighted buoy was placed offshore in 1962; the last officer in charge left in July 1962 (LighthouseFriends). LighthouseFriends gives 1963. No source read supports 1971.
The 30-second flash belonged to the 1870 tower's early years. On 13 June 1922 the characteristic was changed to a 4-second cycle with a 0.8-second flash (Terry Pepper).
The standing brick tower dates from 1870; the first tower of 1855-56 was rubble stone and was replaced.

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-22: story corrected against the cached sources. Removed or reworded: 'bluff' and 'eastern end' (the lead now follows Terry Pepper's 'highest ground on the Point' and LighthouseFriends' location); the 'Anishinaabe history' exhibit (the Forest Service names only the Gnoozhekaaning (Bay Mills Indian Community) exhibit); 'a roadside marker' (a historical marker); the 1868 remedy quoted as Terry Pepper gives it; the Detroit Times ice location (the scan reads 'between Point Aux Plus and Point Iroquois', so 'in the water near Point Iroquois' is not what it says); the L'Anse Sentinel item (credited in its scan to a 'Democrat', not to a Michigan paper's own reporting; the Northerner item is second-hand); the 'Site Closed' off-season wording; 'answer the lake' (the marker's own words are used). Added: the LighthouseFriends 1884 fog bell; the Terry Pepper $18,000 'two new structures' estimate; the lens disagreement (sixth-order in the first tower per LighthouseFriends; Fourth Order from the original tower per Terry Pepper); the 1965 lens removal date; units. first_lit corrected from 1870 to 1856 (the station's first exhibition per Terry Pepper; the 1870 brick tower is a rebuild). Board pages: FY1891 entry on p. 148 (the page header 148 sits above the entry); FY1894 oil house p. 153 and whistle 414 hours p. 158 (scan 210 and 215); FY1896 bell tower scan p. 173. Bulletin 1914: the story's 'William B. Campbell' matches the Bulletin's own 1912-17 index ('Campbell, William B., keeper Point Iroquois, fought fire'), so the Bulletin consistently says B., the roster says L.; still unresolved. The 1914 page image was not rendered (cached PDF is text only). Dates for the first lighting: Terry Pepper says 8 June 1856; the Forest Service says 20 September 1857; the station record cites Rowlett's directory for 1855 (construction). The NRHP nomination (75000940) is a not-digitized placeholder on NPGallery, so it was not read. Heights: Terry Pepper gives 50 ft from foundation to gallery for the 1870 tower; LighthouseFriends about 62 ft; the Forest Service 65 ft; the record 20.0 m. The story uses the Forest Service figure. First lens: Terry Pepper says the fourth-order lens from the original tower was reused in 1870; LighthouseFriends says the original lens was sixth-order and that the 1870 tower had a fourth-order L. Sautter & Cie. lens. Keeper William L. Campbell (roster) vs William B. Campbell (Bulletin 1914): unresolved; the story says so. Fog signal: Terry Pepper dates diaphones to 1926; LighthouseFriends dates an air siren to 1927 and a diaphone to 1933. Campbell and Curtis fire of May 1914 is from the Bulletin and LighthouseFriends. Detroit Times OCR reads 'Point Aux Plus', which the story reads as Point aux Pins; the quote avoids the place name. The L'Anse Sentinel item's OCR is poor; the quote is the phrase 'ill fated Northerner', and the story does not say when the ship was lost. The Smithsonian display of the fourth-order lens was not checked. The Coast Guard Historian's page (archived copy, USCG 'Point Iroquois Lighthouse') was not read; its first-lit year (1871) is not used in the story. The Bay Mills Indian Community exhibit status is from the Forest Service page (closed for renovations, read on the page's own date). The LighthouseFriends Byrnes son's death in 1932 is not used. Roster stints marked 'at least' were kept as given; see the roster's own note.
